analogy.p: Think of the program as a nightclub and the doorman as the validation and authentication code. The doorman checks that you are old enough (a range check), that you have actually shown some ID (a presence check), that the ID is a real card and not a library ticket (a type check) and that it looks like the right layout (a format check). For members-only areas he checks your name against the list (authentication) and only lets you try a few times before turning you away. If you fail, he politely says why and lets you try again. The analogy breaks down because a doorman can use common sense and detect a fake ID that looks right, but validation code can only apply the fixed rules it has been given, so a sensible-looking but false value still gets through.

bullets: **Robust program** = one that carries on working correctly even when given unexpected, incorrect or deliberately harmful input.
The two defensive design considerations in the specification are **anticipating misuse** and **authentication**.
**Input validation** is the main technique used to anticipate misuse of data entry.
Defensive design is done at the **design and coding** stage, not added at the end after problems occur.
The aim is to protect the **program**, the **data** it holds and the **user**.
Good defensive design also means writing clear **error messages** and giving the user another chance to enter data.
It links to **maintainability** and **testing**, which are the other parts of producing robust programs.
core.p: **Defensive design** is the practice of writing programs so that they keep working correctly, and stay secure, even when users do unexpected or harmful things. In J277 section 2.3 (Producing robust programs) it covers two considerations you must know: **anticipating misuse** and **authentication**, together with **input validation**. The idea is that the programmer cannot control what a user types or who tries to log in, so the program itself must be designed to cope. A program that is defensively designed does not crash, does not accept nonsense data and does not let the wrong person in. This is why it is called a **robust** program.

bullets: **Accidental misuse:** typing errors, pressing Enter without typing anything, entering text when a number is required, or an impossible value such as an age of 250.
**Deliberate misuse:** trying to guess a password, trying to enter another person's account, or typing unusual characters to try to damage the program.
Programmers ask 'what could a user enter here?' for **every** input in the program.
Typical defences: **validation** of all inputs, **authentication** to check identity, and **limits** on the number of attempts.
If misuse is not anticipated, the program may **crash**, produce **wrong results**, **corrupt stored data** or allow **unauthorised access**.
Anticipating misuse also includes writing helpful **error messages** that say what was wrong and how to fix it.
Thinking about misuse is part of **planning** and is linked to choosing test data later.
core.p: **Anticipating misuse** means thinking ahead about the ways a program could be used incorrectly, by accident or on purpose, and writing code that handles each one. The programmer imagines the worst-case user: someone who makes typing mistakes, leaves fields blank, enters letters where numbers are needed, or deliberately tries to break in. Each imagined misuse is then guarded against, usually by validation or authentication. Doing this at the design stage is far cheaper than fixing a program after it has crashed or been attacked.

bullets: Validation is carried out by the **computer program** automatically, not by a person.
The five checks you must know are **range**, **length**, **presence**, **type** and **format**.
A failed check should **reject** the data, show an **error message** and let the user **try again**.
Validation can only show data is **reasonable**, never that it is **true or accurate**.
Validation is normally done with a **loop** that repeats until valid data is entered.
Several checks can be **combined** on one input, e.g. a password must be present, long enough and contain a digit.
Validation prevents many **run-time errors**, such as trying to do arithmetic on text.
It is applied to **every** input the user can supply, not just the important ones.
core.h: Input validation: what it is and what it does
core.p: **Input validation** is an automatic check, written into the program, that the data a user enters is **reasonable and sensible** before the program accepts and uses it. If the data fails the check, the program rejects it, displays an error message and asks again. Validation protects the program from bad data that could cause errors, but it is important to understand its limit: validation only checks that data is **acceptable**, not that it is **correct**. An age of 17 passes a range check of 11 to 18 even if the user's real age is 15.

bullets: Definition: checks that data is **within a given range** of values, between a lower and an upper limit.
Example: mark must be **0 to 100**, month must be **1 to 12**, number of players **2 to 4**.
Reject condition in code: **age < 11 OR age > 18** (the OR is needed because a value cannot be both too low and too high).
Accept condition: **age >= 11 AND age <= 18**.
The check only works on **numbers** (or other ordered data), so the type must be correct first.
Dates, times and money amounts often use a range check too, e.g. price must be above 0.
A range check does **not** stop a wrong but in-range value, such as entering 12 instead of 21.
core.p: A **range check** tests that a number lies **between a lowest and a highest acceptable value**. It is used whenever there is a sensible minimum and maximum, such as an exam mark from 0 to 100, an age from 11 to 18, or a month number from 1 to 12. In code it is written by testing that the value is not below the minimum and not above the maximum. The limits themselves are normally **accepted**, so the data 11 and 18 are both valid for a range of 11 to 18, which is why boundary data is important when testing.

bullets: Definition: checks that data is **not too short and/or not too long**, or is an **exact** number of characters.
Example: password **at least 8 characters**; mobile number **exactly 11 digits**.
Code idea: **if len(password) < 8 then** reject and ask again.
A length check says nothing about **what** the characters are, so a password of 8 spaces would still pass.
Combine it with a **format check** or other checks when the content also matters.
A maximum length also helps protect the program by stopping **extremely long** input.
Be careful with **inclusive** limits: 'at least 8' means 8 is allowed and 7 is rejected.
core.p: A **length check** tests that the number of characters in the data is **acceptable**, either an exact length, a minimum or a maximum. It is applied to text and to numbers entered as text. Typical uses include a password of at least 8 characters, a user name of no more than 15 characters, a phone number of exactly 11 digits or a postcode of up to 8 characters. In code the length of a string is found with a function such as **len()** and then compared with the limits.

bullets: Definition: checks that **data has been entered** and the field has not been left empty.
Example: the surname box on a form **must not be blank**.
Code idea: **while name == ""** then display an error and ask again.
A presence check is used for **compulsory** fields; optional fields (like a middle name) do not need one.
Entering a single space or random letters will still **pass** a presence check, so combine with other checks.
Presence checks stop later errors such as trying to use **empty data** in a calculation or a search.
It is often the **first** check applied, before range, length, type or format.
core.p: A **presence check** tests that **some data has actually been entered**, so that a required field is not left blank. It is the simplest validation check. It is used wherever a value is compulsory, such as a user name, a surname or an email address. In code it usually compares the input with an empty string and rejects the input if they are equal. It does not check that what was entered makes sense, only that it is not empty.

bullets: Definition: checks that data is of the **right data type** such as integer, real, string or Boolean.
Example: number of tickets must be an **integer**; a name must not be only digits.
Python idea: **if quantity.isdigit()** is True the text contains only digits and can be converted with int().
Text like '3.5' or '-4' fails isdigit(), so be clear what type the question allows.
Without a type check, int(input()) on the word 'ten' causes a **run-time error** that stops the program.
A value can pass a type check but still fail a range check, e.g. the integer 500 for an age.
Do the **type check first**, because a range check on text makes no sense.
core.p: A **type check** tests that the data entered is of the **correct data type**, for example that a quantity is an **integer** and not text or a decimal. It prevents errors that occur when the program tries to use a value as the wrong type, such as adding a number to the letters 'abc', which would crash the program. Because keyboard input arrives as **text (a string)**, programs often need to check that the characters are all digits before converting with int(). Most languages provide a way to test this, such as isdigit() in Python.

bullets: Definition: checks that data is **in the correct pattern or layout**.
Example: date **dd/mm/yyyy** (two digits, slash, two digits, slash, four digits).
Example: product code of **two letters then three digits**, e.g. AB123.
Example: an email address must contain **@** and a full stop after it.
Code idea (Python): code[0:2].isalpha() and code[2:5].isdigit() and len(code) == 5.
A correctly formatted value can still be **wrong**: 31/02/2024 matches dd/mm/yyyy but is not a real date.
Format checks are often combined with a **length check** to make sure nothing extra is typed.
core.p: A **format check** tests that the data **follows a required pattern**, such as a certain mixture and order of letters, digits and symbols. It is used for data with a fixed layout, including dates written dd/mm/yyyy, postcodes, product codes such as two letters followed by three digits, and email addresses which must contain an @ symbol. Format checks are more specific than length checks because they check **what kind of character** appears in **each position**.

bullets: Pattern: **ask once; while the data is invalid: show error and ask again; endwhile**.
Condition for a range check: **while age < 11 OR age > 18**.
Condition for a presence check: **while name == ""**.
Condition for a length check: **while len(password) < 8**.
Combine checks with **OR** in the loop condition because failing **any one** of them makes the input invalid.
The **error message** should say what is wrong and what is allowed, e.g. 'Age must be from 11 to 18'.
Convert input to the right type with int() **after** the type check, otherwise int() can crash on text.
A **do ... until valid** loop is also correct; check which loop the question wants.
core.h: Writing validation code: the loop pattern
core.p: Validation is almost always written as a **loop that repeats while the data is invalid**. The program asks for the data once, then enters a loop whose condition is true when the data is **bad**; inside the loop it displays an **error message** and asks again. When the user finally enters acceptable data the condition becomes false and the loop ends. This means the program cannot move on until it has valid data. The input statement therefore appears **twice**: once before the loop and once inside it. An alternative is a **do ... until** loop that repeats until the data is valid.

bullets: **Exam mark 0 to 100** is a **range check**.
**Password at least 8 characters** is a **length check**.
**Username box cannot be left empty** is a **presence check**.
**Number of children must be a whole number** is a **type check**.
**Postcode like LS1 4AB** or **date dd/mm/yyyy** is a **format check**.
**Email address** can use a **presence check** (not empty) and a **format check** (contains @).
**Phone number of exactly 11 digits** uses a **length check** and a **type check** (all digits).
Remember validation checks are not interchangeable: giving the wrong name loses the mark even if the idea is close.
core.p: In the exam you are often given a piece of data and asked which validation check is suitable, so learn to match the check to the **rule the data must obey**. Ask: is it a number between limits (range), a fixed or minimum count of characters (length), a compulsory field (presence), a particular data type (type) or a fixed pattern (format)? Often the best answer is a **combination**. Always name the check **and** apply it to the data given, because the mark is usually for the application as well as the name.

bullets: Definition: **checking the identity of a user** before giving access to a system or its data.
**Username and password** is the standard GCSE example: both must match the stored record.
Other methods you may know: **biometrics** (fingerprint or face), **PIN**, and **two-factor** codes sent to a phone.
Passwords should be **strong**: long, with a mixture of upper and lower case letters, numbers and symbols, and not easy to guess.
Systems often **limit the number of attempts** (for example three) and then lock the account or add a delay to stop password guessing.
A new password is often entered **twice** to reduce the chance of a typing error, which is a form of verification.
Programs should not show the password on screen as it is typed, and should not store it in **plain text** (storing it scrambled, or hashed, is better practice).
Only **authorised users** should be able to see or change sensitive data, such as the exam marks held by a school.
core.p: **Authentication** is the process of **confirming that a user is who they claim to be**, so that only **authorised** people can access a system or data. The most common method is a **username and password**: the user types both, and the program checks them against the stored records and allows access only if they match. Authentication is a defence against deliberate misuse, as it stops unauthorised users reading, changing or deleting data. It is different from validation, which checks the data is sensible: authentication checks **who the person is**.

bullets: Set **attempts = 0** and **loggedIn = false** before the loop.
Loop condition: **while attempts < 3 AND loggedIn == false**.
Inside the loop: ask for the **username and password**.
Selection: **if user == storedUser AND pw == storedPw then loggedIn = true else attempts = attempts + 1**.
Use **AND** when comparing: **both** the username **and** the password must be correct.
After the loop: **if loggedIn then** grant access **else** show 'Account locked'.
In real systems the correct details come from a **file or database**, not written into the program; the example hard-codes them to keep it short.
Do not tell the attacker **which** of the user name or password was wrong; just say 'details incorrect'.
core.p: A simple authentication routine reads a user name and a password, compares them with the **stored** values and counts the **failed attempts**. The loop continues while the user is not yet logged in and fewer than the allowed number of attempts have been used. If the details match, a Boolean such as loggedIn is set to true and the loop ends; if not, the attempts counter is increased. After the loop the program tests the result and either grants access or reports that the account is locked. This pattern combines **selection**, **iteration**, a **counter** and a **Boolean flag**.

bullets: **Validation** = automatic check that data is **reasonable** (range, length, presence, type, format).
**Verification** = check that data was **entered correctly**, e.g. double entry or checking against the source.
Validation example: an age of 25 is rejected by a range check of 11 to 18, but an age of 15 passes even if the user's true age is 16.
Verification example: asking the user to **enter the new password twice** and comparing.
**Authentication** answers 'who are you?'; validation answers 'is this data sensible?'.
None of these methods can **prove** data is correct, only reduce the number of errors.
Good robust programs use **several** methods together.
core.h: Validation compared with verification and its limits
core.p: Students often mix up validation with **verification**. **Validation** is the computer checking that data is **reasonable**. **Verification** is checking that data has been **entered correctly**, matching what the user meant, for example by typing an email address or a password twice and comparing the two entries, or by the user proof-reading what they have typed on a confirmation screen. Neither is a complete guarantee. Validation cannot detect a wrong but sensible value, and a double entry can be repeated wrongly, which is why serious systems use both and also rely on authentication to control who can enter data.

bullets: For a range check of **11 to 18**: normal data 15; boundary data **11 and 18** (accepted) and **10 and 19** (rejected).
Invalid or erroneous data for that range: **abc**, a blank entry, **-5**, **200**.
The expected result must be written down **before** running the test, in a test plan.
If 18 is rejected, the programmer probably wrote **< 18** instead of **<= 18** (a logic error).
A **test plan** records test number, purpose, test data, expected result and actual result.
Test every kind of check: presence (empty input), length (too short, exactly right, too long), type (text instead of number) and format (wrong pattern).
Failing tests show **logic errors**; the programmer fixes the code and runs the tests again.
core.h: Testing validation: normal, boundary and invalid data
core.p: Once validation is written it has to be **tested** with carefully chosen data, linking this topic to the testing section of the specification. There are three standard types of test data. **Normal** data is typical valid data that should be accepted. **Boundary** data lies on the edges of the valid range: both the **last accepted** values and the **first rejected** values. **Invalid** (or erroneous) data is of the wrong type or completely outside what is allowed and must be rejected. Testing both sides of each boundary shows whether the programmer used > instead of >= or similar slip-ups.

bullets: **Iteration:** validation is a while or do-until loop that repeats until valid.
**Selection:** if statements test passwords and conditions after the loop.
**Boolean logic:** AND, OR and NOT build the conditions, e.g. age < 11 OR age > 18.
**Data types and casting:** type checks protect int() and float() conversions.
**Strings:** len(), slicing and isdigit()/isalpha() are used for length, format and type checks.
**Testing:** normal, boundary and invalid data check each validation rule; errors found are usually logic errors.
**Maintainability:** comments, meaningful variable names and subprograms (e.g. a validateAge function) keep validation code clear.
**Cyber security:** passwords, authentication and limiting attempts protect against brute-force and unauthorised access.
core.p: Defensive design connects with many other parts of J277 and is a regular source of programming questions, often in 4 to 8 mark questions where you must write a validation loop or name checks. It also connects to the cyber security topic on the other paper, where authentication and strong passwords are used to prevent unauthorised access, and to the idea of maintainability, because defensive code should still be easy to read and update.

exam: **Command words:** 'State' / 'Give' = a short fact; 'Describe' = what the check does with an example; 'Explain' = add a reason ('so that...' / 'because...'); 'Write' / 'Complete' = working code or a flowchart.
**1 mark definitions:** validation = 'an automatic check that data entered is reasonable/sensible'; authentication = 'checking the identity of a user'; each needs the key idea, not just the name.

**Naming checks (1 mark each):** match the rule to the check: limits = range; character count = length; not blank = presence; data type = type; pattern = format. Name it **and** apply it to the data in the question.
**2 marks 'describe a validation check':** the check's name + what it tests + an example, e.g. 'A range check tests the mark is between 0 and 100.'

**Validation code (4 to 6 marks):** input before the loop (1), correct loop condition with OR for a range (1-2), error message inside loop (1), input again inside loop (1), then use of the valid data (1). Keep to the language style of the question.
**Authentication code:** counter starting at 0, loop with limit on attempts, compare username AND password, increase counter on failure, set a flag or output on success, output message after loop.

**Anticipating misuse (2 to 3 marks):** state a possible misuse (blank entry, text instead of number, impossible value, password guessing) and the defence (presence, type or range check, limit on attempts).
**Why validation does not guarantee correct data:** 'the data may be reasonable but still wrong, e.g. a valid age that is not the user's real age'. This is a very common 2 mark question.
**Test data questions:** give normal, boundary and invalid data and say whether each is accepted or rejected; include both sides of the boundary (e.g. 10, 11, 18, 19).
**Spotting errors in validation code:** check the comparison operators (< versus <=), AND versus OR, whether the input is repeated inside the loop and whether the loop condition tests invalid data.
**Model phrases:** 'prevents the program crashing', 'ensures only sensible data is accepted', 'only authorised users can access the data', 'limits the number of attempts to stop guessing'.
**6 mark extended answers:** plan a short list of checks, apply each to a named field, say what error message appears, and finish with testing; use technical terms precisely.

mistakes.r: Validation only checks that data is reasonable or sensible; a wrong but acceptable value, such as age 16 instead of 15, still passes.
mistakes.w: Validation makes sure the data is correct.

mistakes.r: Validation is the computer checking data is reasonable; verification checks data was entered correctly, e.g. entering it twice.
mistakes.w: Validation and verification are the same thing.

mistakes.r: A length check tests the number of characters; a range check tests that a number lies between limits.
mistakes.w: A range check is used to check a password is long enough.

mistakes.r: A number cannot be both below 11 and above 18, so use OR: while age < 11 OR age > 18.
mistakes.w: Use AND to reject an age outside 11 to 18: while age < 11 AND age > 18.

mistakes.r: A presence check only makes sure that something has been entered and the field is not blank.
mistakes.w: A presence check makes sure the data is correct.

mistakes.r: Authentication checks the identity of the user, e.g. with a username and password, so only authorised people gain access.
mistakes.w: Authentication checks that data is sensible.

mistakes.r: Test both sides of each boundary: 11 and 18 are accepted, 10 and 19 are rejected.
mistakes.w: Boundary test data for 11 to 18 is just 11 and 18.

mistakes.r: A good message says what was wrong and what is allowed, e.g. 'Age must be from 11 to 18', then asks again.
Say that the details were incorrect without saying which part, so an attacker learns less.
mistakes.w: Telling the user which of the username or password was wrong.

mistakes.r: int() crashes on text such as 'abc'; check the type (e.g. isdigit) first or the program may stop.
mistakes.w: Converting with int() before checking: age = int(input()) is always safe.

summary: The specification asks you to understand defensive design: anticipating misuse, authenticating users (e.g. username and password), and validating input with range, length, presence, type and format checks, and to write code that does this. It matters because robust programs must cope with accidental and deliberate misuse without crashing or letting the wrong person in.

terms.d: Designing and writing programs so that they cope with unexpected or incorrect input and misuse and continue to work correctly.
A program that continues to work correctly when given unexpected, incorrect or harmful input.
Thinking ahead about how a program could be used wrongly, by accident or deliberately, and writing code to handle it.
An automated check that data entered is reasonable and acceptable before the program uses it.
A validation check that data lies between a lowest and a highest acceptable value.
A validation check that data has an acceptable number of characters.
A validation check that some data has been entered and the field is not empty.
A validation check that data is of the correct data type, such as an integer.
A validation check that data follows a set pattern, such as dd/mm/yyyy.
Confirming that a user is who they claim to be before allowing access to a system or data.
A person who has permission to access a system or particular data.
Checking that data has been entered correctly, for example by typing it twice.
Text displayed to tell the user that their input was invalid and what is allowed.
Test data on the edge of the valid range, including the highest and lowest accepted values and the first values rejected.
Test data of the wrong type or outside the allowed values that must be rejected.
Typical valid test data that the program should accept.
A secret string of characters used with a username to authenticate a user.
A variable that is True or False, used to record whether a condition such as logged in has been met.

worked.ans:
age = int(input("Enter your age (11-18): "))
while age < 11 OR age > 18
   print("Invalid: age must be from 11 to 18")
   age = int(input("Enter your age (11-18): "))
endwhile
print("Age accepted")
Note: a type check (e.g. isdigit) before int() would also stop text input from crashing the program.
worked.q: Write a program that asks the user for their age and keeps asking until a valid age from 11 to 18 inclusive is entered. Display an error message each time the age is invalid. [5]
steps: Ask once before the loop: age = int(input(...)) (1 mark).
The loop must repeat while the age is invalid: age below 11 OR above 18, so while age < 11 OR age > 18 (2 marks: loop and correct condition).
Inside the loop display an error message that tells the user the allowed range (1 mark).
Ask again inside the loop so the value can change (1 mark).
After the loop the valid age can be used or accepted.

worked.ans:
attempts = 0
loggedIn = false
while attempts < 3 AND loggedIn == false
   user = input("Username: ")
   pw = input("Password: ")
   if user == "admin" AND pw == "Green99!" then
      loggedIn = true
   else
      attempts = attempts + 1
      print("Details incorrect")
   endif
endwhile
if loggedIn == true then
   print("Access granted")
else
   print("Account locked")
endif
Attempts are limited so that a person cannot keep guessing passwords until they find the right one (protects against unauthorised access).
worked.q: A program allows a user three attempts to log in. The correct details are stored in username = "admin" and password = "Green99!". Write code for the authentication routine and explain why the number of attempts is limited. [6]
steps: Set attempts = 0 and loggedIn = false (1 mark).
Loop while attempts < 3 AND loggedIn == false (1 mark).
Input username and password inside the loop (1 mark).
Compare both with AND; if correct set loggedIn = true else add 1 to attempts (2 marks).
After the loop output Access granted or Account locked using loggedIn (1 mark).
Reason: limiting attempts stops someone repeatedly guessing the password.

worked.ans: A length check on the password to make sure it has at least 8 characters, and a format check on the date of birth to make sure it follows dd/mm/yyyy. Validation cannot guarantee correctness because it only checks that data is reasonable; a user could enter a date in the correct format that is not their real date of birth and it would still be accepted.
worked.q: A website asks new users to enter a password and a date of birth. Name two different validation checks that could be used, say which field each applies to, and explain why validation cannot guarantee the data is correct. [4]
steps: Password: a length check, e.g. at least 8 characters (check name + field + rule).
Date of birth: a format check (dd/mm/yyyy) or a presence check (field not blank).
Explain the limit: validation checks that data is reasonable, not true.
Give an example such as a date that is valid in format but is not the user's real date of birth.
